data.caption: nutriveen.com
data.copy:
I saw a statistic that made me sick. Children diagnosed with ADHD are four times more likely to die before they turn 30 than children who weren't.

Not twice as likely. Not 3 times. Four.

I didn't believe it when I read it. My brother had been diagnosed with ADHD at six years old and not one doctor had ever mentioned his death.

But here's the truth. Your child's pediatrician tracks their growth. Their psychiatrist tracks their behavior. The thing that's actually killing children with ADHD sits in the middle of all of them... and nobody is paid to look there.

That's why most of us never heard this.

That's why my mother never heard it either.

My brother Tommy was part of that statistic. Twenty-two years on stimulants. Adderall, then Ritalin, then back to Adderall, then the cocaine when the prescriptions stopped working.

Overdose killed him at 28.

I'm 38. Last month my pediatrician told me to put my 10-year-old son on the same medication that started Tommy down that road. I refused.

And what I found instead... in an Amish farming community in Pennsylvania… took my son from a child I dreaded waking up every morning, who'd melt down over anything, who only wanted sugar — to a child I only have to ask once, who eats real food, who comes home and tells me about his day. No Adderall. Nothing my brother ever took.

But to understand why I was desperate enough to drive six hours to an Amish farm at 6 AM, you have to know what I watched ADHD medication do to my brother. And what I didn't know it was quietly doing to me too.

========

It started in first grade. He couldn't sit still. The teacher called my parents. The pediatrician called it ADHD. Wrote the first prescription. Adderall, 5mg. Tommy was six years old.

The first year, the school stopped calling. My mother cried with relief.

data.caption: tryclaritypro.co.uk
data.copy:
I was two seconds away from sending these back. Three days in and I'm thinking, what is this junk? £69 down the drain. Or so I thought.

But I'm getting ahead of myself. Let me start from the beginning.

I'm 71. Retired builder. Built half the houses on the new development off the A46. Forty-three years, rain or shine.

The hearing went gradually. You don't notice at first. People mumble. The TV speakers aren't what they used to be. Restaurants are too loud.

Margaret noticed before I did. Course she did.

'Jim, you've got the TV on thirty-eight.'

'It's fine.'

'The neighbours can hear Antiques Roadshow through the wall.'

But it wasn't fine. I knew it wasn't fine.

Family dinners were the worst. Twelve of us round the table. Everyone talking. Me, smiling and nodding. Catching maybe one word in five. My grandson Oliver telling some story about school. Me, laughing when everyone else laughed.

'Grandad's gone quiet,' my daughter said at our last family dinner.

I hadn't gone quiet. I'd gone deaf.

The NHS waiting list was sixteen months. Boots wanted £3,995. Specsavers, £1,995.

Did what every desperate old man does. Amazon. £59 hearing aids.

SCREEEEEECH. Feedback. Whistling. Everything loud except voices. Sent them back within a week.

For a year and a half, I did nothing. Stopped going to quiz night. Stopped answering the phone. Margaret started ordering for me in restaurants.

The lowest point: Oliver's school play. Front row. Watched his mouth move for forty minutes.

'Did you hear my bit about the pirate, Grandad?'

'Great, mate.'

He was seven. He knew I was lying.

Then Terry from the pub sent me an article.

'Read this, you deaf old fool,' his text said.

Some hearing specialist, worked as an audiologist for thirty years, had taken apart a £3,995 hearing aid from a private clinic. Opened it up. Showed what was actually inside.

And what was inside made me sick.

A tiny chip. A tiny speaker. A tiny microphone. That's it. That's what's in a four thousand…
